category.name: AWS
category.description: Incidents in Amazon Web Services accounts: IAM, S3, EC2, Lambda, KMS, networking, and organization-level abuse.

playbooks.name: AWS access key leaked in a public GitHub repository
playbooks.summary: Use when GitHub secret scanning, AWS Health (AWSCompromisedKeyQuarantine), or a researcher reports an AWS access key ID and secret committed to a public repository.

preparation: Enable GitHub secret scanning and push protection on every org repository
Subscribe the SOC mailbox to AWS Health events for AWSCompromisedKeyQuarantine notices
Keep an inventory mapping every IAM user access key to an owner and purpose
Confirm CloudTrail management events are delivered to Splunk from all regions
identification: Record the leaked key ID, commit SHA, repository URL, and time the commit became public
Run aws iam get-access-key-last-used on the key ID to confirm whether it was ever used
Search CloudTrail by userIdentity.accessKeyId for every API call since the commit time
Check whether AWS attached the AWSCompromisedKeyQuarantineV2 policy to the owning user
List any CreateUser, CreateAccessKey, or CreateLoginProfile calls made with the leaked key
containment: Set the leaked access key to Inactive with aws iam update-access-key
Attach an explicit deny-all inline policy to the owning IAM user while scoping
Revoke any IAM users, keys, or login profiles the leaked key created
Ask the repository owner to make the repo private while the secret is purged
eradication: Delete the leaked access key after confirming the workload has a replacement
Rewrite repository history with git filter-repo and force-push to remove the secret
Search all org repositories and forks for other copies of the same key ID
Remove EC2 instances, Lambda functions, or roles created by the attacker in any region
recovery: Move the workload from a static IAM user key to an IAM role or OIDC federation
Detach the quarantine policy only after the replacement credential is verified
Monitor CloudTrail for the old key ID for 30 days to catch retry attempts
lessons: Measure minutes from public commit to key deactivation and set a target
Decide whether long-lived IAM user keys should be banned by SCP for this account
Add a pre-commit secret scanning hook to the developer workstation baseline

splunk.title: All API calls made with the leaked access key
splunk.spl: index=aws sourcetype=aws:cloudtrail userIdentity.accessKeyId=<leaked_key_id> | stats count min(_time) as first max(_time) as last values(eventName) as actions values(awsRegion) as regions by sourceIPAddress, userAgent | convert ctime(first) ctime(last) | sort - count

splunk.title: Persistence created by the leaked key
splunk.spl: index=aws sourcetype=aws:cloudtrail userIdentity.accessKeyId=<leaked_key_id> eventName IN (CreateUser, CreateAccessKey, CreateLoginProfile, AttachUserPolicy, PutUserPolicy, CreateRole, RunInstances) | table _time eventName awsRegion sourceIPAddress requestParameters.userName requestParameters.roleName errorCode

playbooks.name: AWS access key used from an unknown IP address
playbooks.summary: Use when an IAM user or role access key makes API calls from an IP, ASN, or country never seen for that identity, such as a GuardDuty UnauthorizedAccess:IAMUser/InstanceCredentialExfiltration or anomalous behavior finding.

preparation: Maintain a list of corporate egress IPs, VPN ranges, and CI runner NAT addresses
Baseline normal source IPs and user agents for each IAM user with programmatic keys
Enable GuardDuty in every region so anomalous API findings are generated
identification: Look up the source IP's ASN and geolocation and compare with the identity's baseline
Compare the userAgent string on suspicious calls with the identity's usual SDK or CLI
Check whether the first call from the new IP was sts:GetCallerIdentity reconnaissance
Enumerate read calls such as ListBuckets, DescribeInstances, and GetSecretValue from the IP
Ask the key owner whether they travelled, used a new laptop, or ran a new pipeline
containment: Deactivate the access key used from the unknown IP
Add an aws:SourceIp deny condition to the user's policies for the unknown IP range
Revoke active sessions for any role the key assumed using the Revoke active sessions action
eradication: Find how the key left its intended host: workstation, CI variable, or config file
Rotate any secrets the attacker read via Secrets Manager or SSM Parameter Store
Delete resources created from the unknown IP after preserving their metadata
recovery: Issue a new access key to the legitimate owner and update the dependent service
Confirm the service runs normally with the new key and no errors in CloudTrail
Add the identity to a watchlist for new source IPs for two weeks
lessons: Evaluate an IP-restricted condition on programmatic users that only run from known hosts
Tune a detection for first-seen source ASN per IAM principal
Record where the key was stored and remove that storage pattern org-wide

splunk.title: First-seen source IPs per IAM principal in the last day
splunk.spl: index=aws sourcetype=aws:cloudtrail userIdentity.type IN (IAMUser, AssumedRole) earliest=-30d | stats min(_time) as first_seen count by userIdentity.arn, sourceIPAddress | where first_seen > relative_time(now(), "-1d") | convert ctime(first_seen) | sort - count

splunk.title: Activity from the unknown IP across all identities
splunk.spl: index=aws sourcetype=aws:cloudtrail sourceIPAddress=<ioc_ip> | stats count values(eventName) as actions values(errorCode) as errors by userIdentity.arn, userIdentity.accessKeyId, userAgent, awsRegion

splunk.title: GuardDuty credential anomaly findings
splunk.spl: index=aws sourcetype=aws:cloudwatch:guardduty (detail.type="UnauthorizedAccess:IAMUser/*" OR detail.type="*AnomalousBehavior*") | table _time detail.type detail.severity detail.resource.accessKeyDetails.userName detail.service.action.awsApiCallAction.remoteIpDetails.ipAddressV4

playbooks.name: AWS root account console sign-in
playbooks.summary: Use when CloudTrail shows a ConsoleLogin or API call by the root user of any account, which should almost never happen outside break-glass procedures.

preparation: Store root credentials and hardware MFA in a sealed break-glass process with named custodians
Set root email addresses to monitored distribution lists, not individual mailboxes
Alert in real time on any CloudTrail event where userIdentity.type is Root
Document which accounts in the organization still have root credentials versus centralized root access
identification: Confirm the ConsoleLogin result, MFAUsed value, and source IP for the root sign-in
Check the break-glass log for an approved root access request at that time
List every action the root session performed after sign-in, including billing and IAM changes
Check for a recent PasswordRecoveryRequested or root email change before the sign-in
containment: Reset the root password from the custodian's sealed process if the sign-in was unapproved
Deregister and re-enroll root MFA devices, keeping only custodian-held hardware tokens
Delete any root access keys created during the session
Secure the root email mailbox and check it for forwarding rules
eradication: Revert account settings changed by root, such as contact info, alternate contacts, or support plan
Remove IAM users, roles, or policies created by the root session
Close the gap that allowed sign-in, such as a shared root password in a vault
recovery: Verify the account's billing and contact settings match the organization records
Use Organizations centralized root access to remove root credentials from member accounts
Confirm root activity alerts fire by testing them during the next break-glass drill
lessons: Review who knew the root password and reduce the custodian list
Record whether the alert reached a human within five minutes of sign-in
Decide whether this account should have root credentials at all

splunk.title: Root user sign-ins and API calls
splunk.spl: index=aws sourcetype=aws:cloudtrail userIdentity.type=Root | eval mfa='additionalEventData.MFAUsed' | table _time recipientAccountId eventName sourceIPAddress userAgent mfa responseElements.ConsoleLogin errorMessage

splunk.title: Changes made by root after sign-in
splunk.spl: index=aws sourcetype=aws:cloudtrail userIdentity.type=Root readOnly=false | stats count values(eventName) as changes by recipientAccountId, eventSource | sort - count

playbooks.name: New IAM user created with AdministratorAccess
playbooks.summary: Use when CloudTrail shows CreateUser followed by AttachUserPolicy with AdministratorAccess or an inline Action * policy, outside the normal infrastructure-as-code pipeline.

preparation: Ensure IAM users are only created by the Terraform or CloudFormation pipeline role
Alert on AttachUserPolicy where policyArn ends in AdministratorAccess
Keep an IAM credential report export from each account for comparison
identification: Identify the principal that called CreateUser and AttachUserPolicy and its source IP
Check whether the new user name matches any approved change ticket or IaC commit
Find whether CreateAccessKey or CreateLoginProfile was called for the new user
Search for activity performed by the new user since creation
Look for other IAM users created by the same principal in other accounts
containment: Deactivate the new user's access keys and delete its login profile
Attach an explicit deny-all policy to the new user to stop further use
Restrict the creating principal if it is not the approved IaC role
eradication: Detach AdministratorAccess and delete the rogue IAM user after evidence capture
Investigate how the creating principal was compromised and remediate that credential
Remove any resources or roles provisioned by the rogue user
recovery: Compare the current IAM credential report with the pre-incident export
Run IAM Access Analyzer to confirm no unexpected admin principals remain
Notify the account owner of the final IAM state
lessons: Add an SCP denying iam:CreateUser to every principal except the IaC role
Measure time from CreateUser to detection and alert routing
Consider requiring a permissions boundary on all newly created IAM users

splunk.title: Users created and granted admin
splunk.spl: index=aws sourcetype=aws:cloudtrail eventName IN (CreateUser, AttachUserPolicy, PutUserPolicy, AddUserToGroup) | eval target=coalesce('requestParameters.userName', 'requestParameters.groupName') | stats values(eventName) as actions values(requestParameters.policyArn) as policies min(_time) as first by target, userIdentity.arn, sourceIPAddress | search policies=*AdministratorAccess* OR actions=PutUserPolicy

splunk.title: Activity by the new IAM user
splunk.spl: index=aws sourcetype=aws:cloudtrail userIdentity.userName=<new_user> | stats count values(eventName) as actions by sourceIPAddress, awsRegion, userAgent

playbooks.name: CloudTrail trail stopped, deleted, or modified
playbooks.summary: Use when CloudTrail StopLogging, DeleteTrail, UpdateTrail, or PutEventSelectors removes audit coverage, which often precedes further attacker activity.

preparation: Use an organization trail owned by the management account that member accounts cannot modify
Deliver CloudTrail to a dedicated log archive account with S3 Object Lock
Alert when an expected trail stops sending events to Splunk for more than 30 minutes
identification: Identify who called StopLogging, DeleteTrail, UpdateTrail, or PutEventSelectors and from where
Determine the exact gap window in CloudTrail delivery for each affected region
Check whether the change removed data events, management events, or a whole region
Use CloudTrail Lake or the 90-day Event history to recover events during the gap
Review what the same principal did immediately before and after the logging change
containment: Restart logging with aws cloudtrail start-logging on the affected trail
Revoke the principal's sessions and deactivate its access keys
Recreate a deleted trail with the original S3 bucket, KMS key, and event selectors
eradication: Investigate actions taken during the gap using Event history and service-specific logs
Remove any changes the attacker made while logging was disabled
Check the trail's S3 bucket policy and KMS key policy for tampering
recovery: Confirm new events from every region arrive in Splunk after the restart
Validate log file integrity with aws cloudtrail validate-logs for the affected period
Document the unrecoverable gap in the incident record
lessons: Add an SCP denying cloudtrail:StopLogging and DeleteTrail outside the security account
Track how long the logging gap went unnoticed
Add a delivery-latency health check for each trail

splunk.title: Trail tampering events
splunk.spl: index=aws sourcetype=aws:cloudtrail eventSource=cloudtrail.amazonaws.com eventName IN (StopLogging, DeleteTrail, UpdateTrail, PutEventSelectors, PutInsightSelectors) | table _time recipientAccountId awsRegion eventName userIdentity.arn sourceIPAddress requestParameters.name errorCode

splunk.title: CloudTrail delivery gaps by account and region
splunk.spl: | tstats count where index=aws sourcetype=aws:cloudtrail by _time span=10m, recipientAccountId, awsRegion | where count=0 OR isnull(count) | stats count as empty_buckets by recipientAccountId, awsRegion

splunk.title: Actions by the tampering principal around the change
splunk.spl: index=aws sourcetype=aws:cloudtrail userIdentity.arn=<suspect_arn> earliest=-24h | stats count values(eventName) as actions by eventSource, awsRegion | sort - count

playbooks.name: GuardDuty detector disabled or findings suppressed
playbooks.summary: Use when GuardDuty is disabled, deleted, has its member accounts disassociated, or gains a new suppression rule or trusted IP list that hides findings.

preparation: Use a delegated GuardDuty administrator account with auto-enable for all members
Alert on GuardDuty DeleteDetector, UpdateDetector, and CreateFilter events
Export a baseline of each region's detector settings, filters, and IP sets
identification: Identify the principal that called DeleteDetector, UpdateDetector, or DisassociateFromMasterAccount
List any new suppression filters with CreateFilter and inspect their criteria
Check for CreateIPSet or UpdateIPSet adding a trusted IP list that suppresses findings
Determine which regions and accounts lost GuardDuty coverage and for how long
containment: Re-enable the detector in each affected region from the delegated admin account
Revoke the sessions of the principal that disabled GuardDuty
Delete unauthorized suppression filters and trusted IP sets
eradication: Review findings archived by the rogue filter to see what the attacker hid
Hunt CloudTrail for activity the hidden findings would have flagged
Remediate the access path that allowed the principal to modify GuardDuty
recovery: Confirm findings are flowing to Security Hub and Splunk from every region
Generate sample findings with CreateSampleFindings to validate the pipeline
Reconcile detector settings against the saved baseline
lessons: Add an SCP denying guardduty:DeleteDetector and DisassociateFromAdministratorAccount
Require change approval for any new GuardDuty filter
Measure detection time for loss of a security service

splunk.title: GuardDuty configuration changes
splunk.spl: index=aws sourcetype=aws:cloudtrail eventSource=guardduty.amazonaws.com eventName IN (DeleteDetector, UpdateDetector, CreateFilter, UpdateFilter, CreateIPSet, UpdateIPSet, DisassociateFromMasterAccount, DisassociateFromAdministratorAccount, StopMonitoringMembers) | table _time recipientAccountId awsRegion eventName userIdentity.arn sourceIPAddress requestParameters

splunk.title: Regions that stopped sending GuardDuty findings
splunk.spl: index=aws sourcetype=aws:cloudwatch:guardduty earliest=-14d | stats max(_time) as last_finding by detail.accountId, detail.region | where last_finding < relative_time(now(), "-2d") | convert ctime(last_finding)

playbooks.name: S3 bucket made public through ACL or bucket policy
playbooks.summary: Use when an S3 bucket's Block Public Access is removed, a policy grants Principal *, or an ACL grants AllUsers, exposing objects to the internet.

preparation: Enable account-level S3 Block Public Access in every account by default
Classify buckets by data sensitivity with tags such as data-class
Enable S3 server access logging or CloudTrail data events on sensitive buckets
identification: Find the PutBucketPolicy, PutBucketAcl, or DeletePublicAccessBlock call and its caller
Read the resulting bucket policy and confirm which actions Principal * received
Determine the data classification of objects in the exposed bucket
Query S3 access logs for anonymous GetObject requests during the exposure window
Check whether IAM Access Analyzer raised a public access finding for the bucket
containment: Re-enable Block Public Access on the bucket with put-public-access-block
Remove the public statement from the bucket policy and reset ACLs to private
Disable ACLs by setting Object Ownership to BucketOwnerEnforced
eradication: Confirm whether the change was a mistake or a compromised principal and handle accordingly
Rotate any credentials or keys stored as objects in the exposed bucket
Remove any public objects uploaded by anonymous users if write access was granted
recovery: Move intentionally public content to CloudFront with origin access control
Re-run Access Analyzer to confirm the bucket has no public findings
Engage privacy or legal if regulated data was downloaded anonymously
lessons: Add an SCP denying s3:PutAccountPublicAccessBlock changes by non-security roles
Track the exposure window from policy change to remediation
Add a Config rule for s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited with auto-remediation

splunk.title: Bucket permission changes that may grant public access
splunk.spl: index=aws sourcetype=aws:cloudtrail eventSource=s3.amazonaws.com eventName IN (PutBucketPolicy, PutBucketAcl, DeleteBucketPublicAccessBlock, PutBucketPublicAccessBlock, PutObjectAcl) | table _time requestParameters.bucketName eventName userIdentity.arn sourceIPAddress requestParameters.bucketPolicy

splunk.title: Anonymous reads from the exposed bucket
splunk.spl: index=aws sourcetype=aws:s3:accesslogs bucket_name=<bucket> operation=REST.GET.OBJECT requester="-" | stats count sum(bytes_sent) as bytes dc(key) as objects by remote_ip | sort - bytes

playbooks.name: Mass data download from an S3 bucket
playbooks.summary: Use when a principal downloads an unusual volume or number of S3 objects, such as a GuardDuty Exfiltration:S3/AnomalousBehavior finding or a sudden spike in GetObject bytes.

preparation: Enable CloudTrail S3 data events for buckets tagged as sensitive
Enable GuardDuty S3 Protection in every account
Baseline daily GetObject volume per principal for sensitive buckets
identification: Quantify objects, bytes, and prefixes read by the principal during the spike
Identify the source IPs and whether they belong to a VPC endpoint or the internet
Check whether the principal also called ListObjectsV2 across many prefixes beforehand
Determine whether the principal is a human, application role, or replication job
Look for CopyObject or replication configuration sending data to another account
containment: Revoke the principal's active sessions or deactivate its access key
Add a bucket policy deny for the principal ARN on s3:GetObject
Restrict bucket access to the VPC endpoint with an aws:SourceVpce condition
eradication: Identify and remediate how the principal's credentials were obtained
Remove replication rules or batch operations jobs created by the attacker
Rotate secrets or keys contained in the downloaded objects
recovery: Restore normal access for legitimate workloads with least-privilege prefixes
Produce a list of downloaded object keys for the data owner and legal review
Keep GuardDuty S3 Protection alerts for the bucket at high priority for 30 days
lessons: Decide whether sensitive buckets should be reachable only through VPC endpoints
Add a volume threshold detection on bytes_sent per principal per hour
Review whether the principal needed read access to the whole bucket

splunk.title: Top S3 readers by bytes from access logs
splunk.spl: index=aws sourcetype=aws:s3:accesslogs operation=REST.GET.OBJECT bucket_name=<bucket> | stats sum(bytes_sent) as bytes dc(key) as objects by requester, remote_ip | eval GB=round(bytes/1024/1024/1024,2) | sort - bytes

splunk.title: GetObject data events by principal per hour
splunk.spl: index=aws sourcetype=aws:cloudtrail eventSource=s3.amazonaws.com eventName=GetObject requestParameters.bucketName=<bucket> | timechart span=1h count by userIdentity.arn limit=10

splunk.title: S3 exfiltration GuardDuty findings
splunk.spl: index=aws sourcetype=aws:cloudwatch:guardduty detail.type="Exfiltration:S3/*" | table _time detail.type detail.severity detail.resource.s3BucketDetails{}.name detail.resource.accessKeyDetails.principalId

playbooks.name: S3 ransom: objects deleted or encrypted and ransom note left
playbooks.summary: Use when S3 objects are mass-deleted, overwritten, or re-encrypted with an attacker KMS key and a ransom note object appears in the bucket.

preparation: Enable S3 Versioning and Object Lock on buckets holding critical data
Back up critical buckets with AWS Backup to a separate account with a vault lock
Enable CloudTrail data events for DeleteObject and PutObject on critical buckets
identification: Retrieve the ransom note object and record its key, contents, and uploader
Count DeleteObject, DeleteObjects, and PutObject calls by principal during the event
Check whether versioning was suspended with PutBucketVersioning before deletion
Determine whether objects were re-encrypted with SSE-C or an external KMS key
Check for PutBucketLifecycleConfiguration rules that expire noncurrent versions
containment: Revoke the principal's credentials and attach a deny-all policy to it
Add a bucket policy deny on s3:DeleteObject and s3:PutLifecycleConfiguration for all but the security role
Delete attacker lifecycle rules immediately to stop expiry of old versions
Do not contact the extortion address; route communications through legal
eradication: Remove the attacker's access path, such as a leaked key or compromised role
Delete the ransom note object after preserving a copy as evidence
Remove any attacker-added KMS grants or cross-account bucket permissions
recovery: Restore prior object versions by removing delete markers with a batch job
Restore from AWS Backup where versions were permanently deleted
Validate restored object counts and checksums against inventory reports
Re-enable versioning and confirm Object Lock retention on the bucket
lessons: Report which buckets lacked versioning or backup and fix them
Add an alert on PutBucketVersioning with status Suspended
Measure recovery time objective achieved versus target

splunk.title: Mass deletions and overwrites by principal
splunk.spl: index=aws sourcetype=aws:cloudtrail eventSource=s3.amazonaws.com eventName IN (DeleteObject, DeleteObjects, PutObject, CopyObject) requestParameters.bucketName=<bucket> | timechart span=5m count by eventName

splunk.title: Versioning, lifecycle, and encryption tampering
splunk.spl: index=aws sourcetype=aws:cloudtrail eventSource=s3.amazonaws.com eventName IN (PutBucketVersioning, PutBucketLifecycle, PutBucketLifecycleConfiguration, PutBucketEncryption, PutBucketReplication) | table _time requestParameters.bucketName eventName userIdentity.arn sourceIPAddress requestParameters

splunk.title: Ransom note uploads
splunk.spl: index=aws sourcetype=aws:s3:accesslogs operation=REST.PUT.OBJECT (key=*README* OR key=*RECOVER* OR key=*ransom* OR key=*.txt) | table _time bucket_name key requester remote_ip

playbooks.name: EC2 instances launched for cryptocurrency mining
playbooks.summary: Use when GuardDuty reports CryptoCurrency:EC2/BitcoinTool or many large GPU or compute instances are launched unexpectedly, often in unused regions.

preparation: Set EC2 service quotas for GPU instance families low in accounts that do not use them
Configure AWS Budgets alerts on daily EC2 spend per account
Restrict usable regions with an SCP on aws:RequestedRegion
identification: List RunInstances calls by instance type, region, and calling principal
Retrieve the user data from the launched instances to see the miner bootstrap script
Check VPC flow logs for outbound connections to mining pool ports such as 3333 and 4444
Check whether new key pairs or security groups were created alongside the instances
Determine whether the instances came from a compromised key or an existing instance's role
containment: Stop the mining instances after capturing EBS snapshots for evidence
Revoke the credentials that called RunInstances
Block mining pool destinations at the network firewall or via NACL
eradication: Terminate the instances and delete attacker key pairs, security groups, and AMIs
Cancel spot fleet requests and launch templates created by the attacker
Sweep every region for remaining attacker resources with a tag or creator search
recovery: Open an AWS Support case to request review of fraudulent charges
Restore service quotas to the reduced baseline
Confirm daily spend has returned to normal in Cost Explorer
lessons: Record which unused regions were abused and deny them by SCP
Add a detection on RunInstances for GPU families such as p3, p4, and g5
Measure cost incurred before detection

splunk.title: Instance launches by type and region
splunk.spl: index=aws sourcetype=aws:cloudtrail eventName=RunInstances NOT errorCode=* | stats count sum(requestParameters.instancesSet.items{}.maxCount) as requested values(requestParameters.instanceType) as types by awsRegion, userIdentity.arn, sourceIPAddress | sort - count

splunk.title: Outbound traffic to common mining pool ports
splunk.spl: index=aws sourcetype=aws:cloudwatchlogs:vpcflow dest_port IN (3333, 4444, 5555, 7777, 14444, 45700) action=ACCEPT | stats sum(bytes) as bytes dc(dest_ip) as pools by src_ip, dest_port | sort - bytes

splunk.title: Cryptocurrency GuardDuty findings
splunk.spl: index=aws sourcetype=aws:cloudwatch:guardduty detail.type="CryptoCurrency:*" | table _time detail.region detail.type detail.resource.instanceDetails.instanceId detail.resource.instanceDetails.instanceType

playbooks.name: EC2 instance role credentials stolen via SSRF to IMDS
playbooks.summary: Use when a web application's SSRF flaw is used to read instance role credentials from 169.254.169.254, and those credentials are then used from outside the instance.

preparation: Enforce IMDSv2 with HttpTokens required on all instances and launch templates
Log web application requests including full URL parameters to Splunk
Enable GuardDuty findings for InstanceCredentialExfiltration.OutsideAWS
identification: Search web logs for request parameters containing 169.254.169.254 or metadata paths
Confirm whether the instance still allowed IMDSv1 at the time of the request
Find CloudTrail calls by the instance role session made from IPs that are not the instance
List the APIs the stolen role session called and resources it touched
Identify the vulnerable application endpoint and parameter used for SSRF
containment: Revoke active sessions on the instance role with an aws:TokenIssueTime deny policy
Set HttpTokens to required on the instance with modify-instance-metadata-options
Block the SSRF endpoint at the WAF or load balancer while a fix is prepared
eradication: Patch the application to validate and allowlist outbound URLs
Reduce the instance role's permissions to what the application actually needs
Remove resources or persistence created with the stolen role credentials
recovery: Redeploy the patched application and confirm SSRF test payloads are rejected
Confirm no further role usage from external IPs in CloudTrail
Set the account default IMDS setting to IMDSv2 only
lessons: Add a detection for instance role credentials used from non-EC2 source IPs
Add SSRF test cases to the application security test suite
Count instances still allowing IMDSv1 and set a deadline to remove them

splunk.title: Web requests containing metadata service addresses
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where (Web.url="*169.254.169.254*" OR Web.url="*latest/meta-data*" OR Web.url="*iam/security-credentials*") by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url | sort - count

splunk.title: Instance role sessions used from outside the instance
splunk.spl: index=aws sourcetype=aws:cloudtrail userIdentity.type=AssumedRole userIdentity.principalId=*:i-* | rex field=userIdentity.principalId ":(?<instance_id>i-[0-9a-f]+)" | stats values(sourceIPAddress) as src values(eventName) as actions by instance_id, userIdentity.sessionContext.sessionIssuer.arn | where mvcount(src)>1

splunk.title: GuardDuty instance credential exfiltration
splunk.spl: index=aws sourcetype=aws:cloudwatch:guardduty detail.type="UnauthorizedAccess:IAMUser/InstanceCredentialExfiltration*" | table _time detail.type detail.resource.accessKeyDetails.userName detail.service.action.awsApiCallAction.api detail.service.action.awsApiCallAction.remoteIpDetails.ipAddressV4

playbooks.name: Lambda function backdoored or created for persistence
playbooks.summary: Use when a Lambda function's code, layers, environment, or resource policy is changed unexpectedly, or a new function with a public function URL or EventBridge trigger appears.

preparation: Require Lambda code signing for production functions
Deploy functions only through a CI pipeline role and alert on other UpdateFunctionCode callers
Keep function code hashes from each release for comparison
identification: List UpdateFunctionCode, UpdateFunctionConfiguration, and CreateFunction calls by principal
Compare the current CodeSha256 with the hash from the last pipeline deployment
Download the function package and review it for outbound callbacks or credential dumping
Check AddPermission and CreateFunctionUrlConfig for public or cross-account invoke grants
Inspect new layers and EventBridge rules attached to the function
containment: Set reserved concurrency to zero on the backdoored function to stop executions
Remove the public function URL and any attacker-added resource policy statements
Disable EventBridge rules or event source mappings created by the attacker
eradication: Redeploy the function from the last known-good pipeline artifact
Delete attacker-created functions, layers, and their execution roles
Rotate secrets the function's environment variables or role could read
recovery: Restore reserved concurrency and confirm the function works through normal triggers
Verify CodeSha256 matches the pipeline artifact after redeployment
Review CloudWatch Logs for the function to confirm no further suspicious invocations
lessons: Enforce code signing configuration with an SCP or Config rule
Add detection for lambda:AddPermission with Principal *
Review which humans can update production function code

splunk.title: Lambda code, config, and permission changes
splunk.spl: index=aws sourcetype=aws:cloudtrail eventSource=lambda.amazonaws.com (eventName=UpdateFunctionCode* OR eventName=UpdateFunctionConfiguration* OR eventName=CreateFunction* OR eventName=AddPermission* OR eventName=CreateFunctionUrlConfig* OR eventName=PublishLayerVersion*) | table _time awsRegion eventName requestParameters.functionName userIdentity.arn sourceIPAddress

splunk.title: Event triggers wired to functions
splunk.spl: index=aws sourcetype=aws:cloudtrail eventName IN (PutRule, PutTargets, CreateEventSourceMapping20150331) | table _time eventName requestParameters.name requestParameters.targets{}.arn requestParameters.functionName userIdentity.arn

playbooks.name: SSM Run Command or Session Manager used to execute on instances
playbooks.summary: Use when SendCommand, StartSession, or new SSM documents are used by an unexpected principal to run scripts on managed EC2 instances or hybrid nodes.

preparation: Send SSM Run Command output and Session Manager logs to S3 and CloudWatch
Restrict ssm:SendCommand to approved roles and specific documents
Keep an allowlist of SSM documents used by operations automation
identification: List SendCommand and StartSession calls by principal, document, and target instances
Retrieve command parameters and output for each suspicious invocation
Check for CreateDocument calls that defined a custom document with shell commands
Review Session Manager transcripts for interactive sessions by the principal
Identify which instances ran the commands and what roles they hold
containment: Revoke the principal's credentials and sessions
Terminate active Session Manager sessions with terminate-session
Cancel pending commands with cancel-command on the affected instances
eradication: Delete attacker-created SSM documents and State Manager associations
Investigate target instances for persistence such as cron jobs, users, or SSH keys
Rebuild instances where commands installed tooling or altered binaries
recovery: Restore operations automation permissions with document-scoped policies
Confirm SSM Agent and logging configuration on rebuilt instances
Verify no further SendCommand from the principal in CloudTrail
lessons: Add detection for SendCommand using AWS-RunShellScript by non-automation principals
Decide whether Session Manager requires an approval workflow
Track how many instances were reachable from the abused principal

splunk.title: Run Command and session activity by principal

playbooks.name: EBS snapshot or AMI shared with an external account
playbooks.summary: Use when ModifySnapshotAttribute or ModifyImageAttribute adds createVolumePermission or launchPermission for an unknown account or makes a snapshot public.

preparation: Enable EBS Block Public Access for snapshots in every region
Maintain a list of AWS account IDs owned by the organization
Alert on ModifySnapshotAttribute with createVolumePermission add

Check the target account IDs against the organization account list
Determine which volume and instance each snapshot came from and its data

containment: Remove the external createVolumePermission with modify-snapshot-attribute remove
Remove launchPermission from any AMIs shared to the same accounts
Revoke the sharing principal's credentials

Rotate credentials, keys, or database passwords stored on the shared volumes
Remediate the compromised principal's access path

playbooks.name: RDS snapshot exfiltrated by sharing or export

Alert on ModifyDBSnapshotAttribute and StartExportTask

Rotate the database master password and application credentials

Review database audit logs for direct queries during the same window
Hand the data inventory to privacy for breach assessment

playbooks.name: KMS key policy changed or key scheduled for deletion

preparation: Inventory customer managed keys and which services and data each key protects
Alert on ScheduleKeyDeletion, DisableKey, and PutKeyPolicy for every key

playbooks.name: AWS Organizations SCP detached or weakened
playbooks.summary: Use when a service control policy is detached from the root or an OU, updated to remove deny statements, or an account is moved out of a restricted OU.

preparation: Store all SCPs in version control and deploy them through a single pipeline
Limit access to the management account to a small, MFA-protected group
Alert on DetachPolicy, UpdatePolicy, DeletePolicy, and MoveAccount in Organizations

Move the account back to its guardrail OU
Revoke the management account session that made the change

Reset credentials for the management account principal involved
Remove any new delegated administrator registrations made by the attacker

Validate guardrails by testing a denied action from a member account

Add drift detection comparing live SCPs with the repository daily

playbooks.name: Cross-account trust added to an IAM role
playbooks.summary: Use when UpdateAssumeRolePolicy or CreateRole adds a trust relationship to an unknown AWS account, a wildcard principal, or a new OIDC or SAML provider.

preparation: Use IAM Access Analyzer with the organization as the zone of trust
Keep a register of approved third-party accounts and their external IDs
Alert on UpdateAssumeRolePolicy and CreateOpenIDConnectProvider

Check the trusted account ID against the organization and vendor register
Determine whether the trust requires sts:ExternalId or MFA conditions

Revoke active sessions for the role with a token issue time deny
Delete any rogue OIDC or SAML identity providers added alongside

playbooks.name: Mass read of Secrets Manager secrets or SSM parameters
playbooks.summary: Use when one principal calls GetSecretValue or GetParameters with decryption on many secrets in a short window, suggesting credential harvesting.

preparation: Scope secretsmanager:GetSecretValue in policies to specific secret ARNs per workload
Tag each secret with the owning application and rotation contact

Check whether ListSecrets or DescribeParameters enumeration preceded the reads

Add a resource policy deny on the most sensitive secrets for the principal

Find how the principal was compromised and close that path
Check downstream systems for logins with the harvested credentials

playbooks.name: Amazon Cognito user pool or identity pool abused

playbooks.name: Security group opened to 0.0.0.0/0 on SSH or RDP

Add a detection on repeated ConsoleLogin failures followed by success
Review whether the MFA-enforcement policy was attached to this user

splunk.title: Console sign-ins without MFA
splunk.spl: index=aws sourcetype=aws:cloudtrail eventName=ConsoleLogin userIdentity.type=IAMUser additionalEventData.MFAUsed=No | stats count min(_time) as first max(_time) as last values(responseElements.ConsoleLogin) as results by userIdentity.userName, sourceIPAddress, userAgent | convert ctime(first) ctime(last)

splunk.title: Failed then successful console sign-ins
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.app=*signin.amazonaws.com* by Authentication.user, Authentication.src, Authentication.action | xyseries Authentication.user Authentication.action count | where failure > 5 AND success > 0

playbooks.name: IAM Identity Center user or configuration compromised
playbooks.summary: Use when an attacker gains control of an IAM Identity Center user, changes the identity source, creates permission sets, or assigns admin access across accounts in the organization.

preparation: Integrate Identity Center with the corporate IdP and require phishing-resistant MFA there
Restrict Identity Center administration to a delegated admin account with few operators
Alert on CreateAccountAssignment, CreatePermissionSet, and identity source changes
identification: List CreateAccountAssignment events and the principals and permission sets assigned
Check for new or modified permission sets with AdministratorAccess attached
Review sso-directory events for CreateUser, password resets, or MFA device changes
Check whether the identity source or external IdP SAML metadata was changed
List federated sessions created by the compromised user across member accounts
containment: Disable the compromised Identity Center user and revoke its active sessions
Delete unauthorized account assignments with delete-account-assignment
Revert identity source or IdP metadata changes
eradication: Delete rogue permission sets and inline policies added to existing sets
Revoke role sessions in member accounts created through the compromised assignments
Reset the user's IdP credentials and MFA factors
recovery: Reconcile account assignments with the access-request system of record
Reprovision permission sets to all accounts and confirm they match IaC
Confirm legitimate users can still sign in to the access portal
lessons: Require approval workflow for new admin permission set assignments
Add a detection for permission set changes outside the IaC pipeline
Measure how many accounts received the rogue assignment

splunk.title: Identity Center assignment and permission set changes
splunk.spl: index=aws sourcetype=aws:cloudtrail eventSource IN (sso.amazonaws.com, sso-directory.amazonaws.com, identitystore.amazonaws.com) eventName IN (CreateAccountAssignment, CreatePermissionSet, AttachManagedPolicyToPermissionSet, PutInlinePolicyToPermissionSet, ProvisionPermissionSet, CreateUser, UpdatePassword, DeleteMfaDeviceForUser, UpdateExternalIdPConfigurationForDirectory) | table _time eventName requestParameters userIdentity.arn sourceIPAddress

splunk.title: Federated sessions from the suspect user
splunk.spl: index=aws sourcetype=aws:cloudtrail eventName=AssumeRoleWithSAML OR (userIdentity.arn=*AWSReservedSSO* userIdentity.arn=*<suspect_user>*) | stats count values(eventName) as actions by recipientAccountId, userIdentity.arn, sourceIPAddress

playbooks.name: CI/CD deployment role abused from a compromised pipeline
playbooks.summary: Use when a GitHub Actions, GitLab, or Jenkins deployment role is assumed by an unexpected repository, branch, or runner, or performs actions outside its normal deployment pattern.

preparation: Scope OIDC trust policies with token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub to repository and branch
Give each pipeline its own deployment role with least privilege
Baseline the API calls each deployment role makes during a normal release
identification: Check AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity events for the sub claim and identify the repo and ref
Compare the role's API calls against the normal deployment baseline
Review the pipeline run logs and workflow file changes around the time of the session
Identify whether a pull request from a fork or a new branch triggered the run
Look for the role's credentials being used from IPs outside the runner pool
containment: Restrict the role's trust policy to the protected main branch only
Revoke all active sessions for the deployment role
Disable the affected workflow or pipeline until reviewed
eradication: Revert malicious workflow, buildspec, or Jenkinsfile commits
Remove resources and IAM changes the role made outside the release
Rotate long-lived secrets stored in the CI system's variables
recovery: Redeploy the application from a verified commit through the hardened pipeline
Confirm the role's activity matches the deployment baseline on the next release
Require code owner review on workflow file changes
lessons: Audit every OIDC trust policy for wildcard sub conditions
Add a detection for deployment roles calling IAM or STS outside releases
Decide whether self-hosted runners need isolation per repository

splunk.title: Web identity assumptions of the deployment role
splunk.spl: index=aws sourcetype=aws:cloudtrail eventName=AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity requestParameters.roleArn=*<deploy_role>* | table _time userIdentity.userName userIdentity.identityProvider requestParameters.roleSessionName sourceIPAddress responseElements.subjectFromWebIdentityToken

splunk.title: Deployment role actions outside its baseline
splunk.spl: index=aws sourcetype=aws:cloudtrail userIdentity.sessionContext.sessionIssuer.userName=<deploy_role> earliest=-30d latest=-1d | stats count by eventName | fields eventName | eval baseline=1 | append [ search index=aws sourcetype=aws:cloudtrail userIdentity.sessionContext.sessionIssuer.userName=<deploy_role> earliest=-1d | stats count by eventName ] | stats max(baseline) as baseline sum(count) as recent by eventName | where isnull(baseline)

playbooks.name: EKS node IAM role credentials abused from a pod
playbooks.summary: Use when a compromised pod reaches the node's instance metadata to use the EKS node role, or the node role is used for actions outside normal kubelet and ECR pulls.

preparation: Set IMDSv2 hop limit to 1 on EKS node groups so pods cannot reach node credentials
Use EKS Pod Identity or IRSA so workloads never need the node role
Send EKS control plane audit logs to Splunk
identification: Find node role API calls that are not EC2 describe, ECR pull, or EKS describe calls
Identify the node instance ID from the role session name and list pods scheduled there
Check kube audit logs for exec or attach into pods on that node
Review the suspect pod's image and processes for curl to 169.254.169.254
Check whether node role credentials were used from IPs outside the VPC
containment: Cordon and drain the affected node and isolate the suspect pod's namespace with a network policy
Revoke node role sessions issued before now
Apply the hop-limit setting to the node group launch template
eradication: Replace the node with a fresh one from the managed node group
Remove the compromised workload and fix the vulnerability it was exploited through
Remove extra permissions attached to the node role over time
recovery: Move workloads that used node role permissions to Pod Identity
Confirm the node role only performs expected calls after recovery
Run a pod-level IMDS reachability check across clusters
lessons: Add a detection on node role API calls outside the allowed set
Count node groups still using hop limit 2 and fix them
Review pod security standards for the affected namespace

splunk.title: Unusual API calls by EKS node roles
splunk.spl: index=aws sourcetype=aws:cloudtrail userIdentity.sessionContext.sessionIssuer.userName=*NodeInstanceRole* NOT eventName IN (Describe*, GetAuthorizationToken, BatchGetImage, GetDownloadUrlForLayer, BatchCheckLayerAvailability, AssignPrivateIpAddresses, AttachNetworkInterface, CreateNetworkInterface) | stats count values(eventName) as actions by userIdentity.principalId, sourceIPAddress

splunk.title: Exec into pods on the affected node
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype=kube:apiserver:audit objectRef.subresource IN (exec, attach) | table _time user.username objectRef.namespace objectRef.name sourceIPs{} requestURI
